title: Support Vector Machines
interviewAnswer: An SVM finds a decision boundary with maximum margin. Kernel functions allow nonlinear boundaries by computing similarity in an implicit higher-dimensional feature space.
why: SVMs test geometric reasoning, margins, kernels and regularization trade-offs.
intuition: A linear SVM chooses a separating hyperplane with the widest margin to the closest training points. Only support vectors determine the boundary.
deepDive: Soft-margin SVM allows violations controlled by C: large C penalizes mistakes strongly and can reduce margin; small C regularizes more. Kernel SVM uses similarity functions to represent nonlinear boundaries implicitly through the kernel trick. Feature scaling matters because distances/dot products drive the geometry. Kernel methods scale poorly to very large n.
math: min 1/2||w||² + C Σ ξ_i subject to y_i(wᵀx_i+b) ≥ 1-ξ_i
workedExample: An RBF SVM can model a curved decision boundary on a medium-size dataset, but on millions of rows gradient boosting or linear methods may be much more practical.
commonMistakes: Calling C the regularization strength in the same direction as lambda; larger C means weaker regularization.
Skipping feature scaling for distance-based kernels.
Assuming SVM probability outputs are native margins without calibration.
production: Kernel SVM training/inference can become expensive with many support vectors. Monitor scale and calibration if probabilities are needed.
